title: Lawyer Time Tracking Software: How Passive Capture Works and What to Check Before You Buy
summary: See how passive capture works in lawyer time tracking software, what delayed manual entry costs a firm, and what to verify before you buy timekeeping tools.
body_markdown:
### AI Summary


-


Lawyer time tracking software splits into three groups: timer-based tools, activity loggers, and passive AI-native capture. The groups differ on how much of the work the attorney still does by hand.


-


Attorneys who wait until the end of the day to record hours lose around 10% of their billable time, and reconstruction days later loses more.


-


Passive capture connects to the calendar, email, documents, and calls, then drafts a matter-attributed entry the attorney reviews before it posts.


-


Outside counsel guidelines and carrier bill review cut entries that fail coding or narrative rules, so the compliance check belongs at the point of entry.


-


A written buyer's checklist and a pilot on the firm's own matters prove more than any vendor demo.


## Which Tools Capture Time Passively in the Background, and How Accurate Are They?


Passive capture works by connecting to the systems an attorney already works in: the calendar, the email client, document management, call logs, and the applications open on screen. The software matches each piece of activity to a matter, using client names, matter numbers, or file paths, then drafts a narrative describing the work before the attorney ever opens a timesheet.


Two factors separate an accurate system from an approximate one.


1.


The number of connected sources. A tool that only reads the calendar misses the two hours an attorney spent drafting inside a shared document with no calendar entry attached to it. A tool that reads calendar, email, documents, and calls closes most of that gap.


2.


Whether an attorney reviews the drafted entry before it posts to the billing system. The strongest passive systems keep a human in the loop: the entry drafts automatically, but it does not become a bill until someone confirms it.

## Does Passive Capture Hold Up Under Outside Counsel Guidelines (OCGs) and Bill Review?


Most institutional and corporate clients now issue Outside Counsel Guidelines (OCGs) that go beyond a billing rate. They specify task-based codes, prohibit block billing (several tasks lumped into one entry), and require a narrative that describes the actual work rather than restating a code. Carriers and corporate legal departments increasingly review bills through e-billing systems built on the[LEDES format](https://ledes.org/) , the industry standard the[LEDES Oversight Committee](https://ledes.org/) maintains for exchanging billing and financial data between law firms and their clients. An entry that fails to match the guideline on file gets flagged or cut before it ever reaches a partner's desk. Each cut is a write-down, and accumulated write-downs pull the firm's[realization rate](https://pointone.com/blog/blog-law-firm-realization-rate) below its billed rates.


Task-based billing reaches into court-supervised fee review too. The[U.S. Trustee Program's fee guidelines](https://www.justice.gov/ust/Prof_Comp) for attorney compensation in bankruptcy cases have required task-based billing detail since 1996, refined further for large chapter 11 matters in 2013. The standard a corporate client's OCG demands and the standard a bankruptcy court applies to a fee application both point the same direction: detailed, task-coded, same-day entries hold up under review, and reconstructed ones do not.


That is the real test for a passive-capture tool in this category. It is not whether it logs time. It is whether it can apply a specific client's guideline, narrative requirements, prohibited codes, rate caps, automatically at the point of entry, rather than leaving compliance to a pre-bill reviewer working against a deadline. A tool that only logs activity pushes that entire compliance check downstream.[What a defensible narrative needs to include](https://pointone.com/blog/how-to-craft-better-legal-bills) does not change with the tool, and[pre-bill and proformance review](https://pointone.com/blog/optimizing-legal-pre-bill-proforma-review) works as the last catch, not the only catch.

## FAQs about Lawyer Time Tracking Software


Which is the best software to track billable hours?


There is no single best answer across every firm. The better question is which category fits your caseload: a timer if attorneys already track time reliably by hand, an activity logger if you want a record without a drafted narrative, or passive capture if the goal is to stop reconstructing days from memory. Score any specific vendor against the buyer's checklist above rather than a generic "best of" list.


Does passive time tracking work for solo attorneys, or only large firms?


Passive capture applies at any firm size. A solo attorney gains the same benefit a large firm does: entries exist without a manual step, so nothing depends on remembering to log time at the end of a long day. What changes by firm size is which OCG and integration requirements matter most. A solo practitioner cares less about multi-timekeeper coding consistency than a mid-size firm billing under several clients' guidelines at once.


Does automatic time tracking replace timesheets and manual entry completely?


Not entirely, and that is by design. The strongest passive systems still put a human in the loop: the software drafts the entry, but an attorney reviews and approves it before it posts to the billing system. What disappears is the manual step of remembering and typing the entry from scratch, not the attorney's final sign-off.


How long does it take to implement lawyer time tracking software firm-wide?


Timelines vary by firm size, the number of practice management and billing systems it needs to connect to, and how many OCGs need to be loaded before go-live. Set the timeline with the vendor in writing before the contract is signed, and treat retroactive capture as part of that plan so the transition month does not create a gap in the firm's records.


Is passive time-capture software secure, and where is the data stored?


Ask any vendor for a direct link to independent security certifications and a published trust center, not a verbal assurance in a sales call. Your IT team, not your billing team, should review that documentation before a firm-wide decision.


Does lawyer time tracking software integrate with the practice management or billing system we already use?


Check this before anything else on the checklist. A tool that cannot pass entries into your existing billing system without manual re-entry creates a second system of record, which defeats the purpose of automating capture in the first place. Confirm the integration with a real export in your billing system's format, not a screenshot.


What happens to time worked before the software goes live?


Look for retroactive capture: the ability to reconstruct a date range from existing calendar, email, and document activity rather than asking attorneys to remember and re-enter it by hand. Without it, a firm-wide rollout leaves a gap in the record for the weeks before go-live.
